Generative AI without the hype: what it is and what it can really do

A clear explanation of why it can create text, images and code—and why it can also be confidently wrong.

By Juliana Gonzalez · September 8, 2026 · 7 min read

In only a few years, generative artificial intelligence has moved from a specialist topic into tools we use to write, design, code and search for information.

Its outputs can seem human. It can hold a conversation, draft an email, suggest code or create an image from a few lines of text. This may give the impression that it understands and thinks in the same way we do.

Generative AI does not think like a person. It learns patterns and uses them to produce new content.

What is generative artificial intelligence?

Generative AI includes systems capable of creating content in response to an instruction. That content can be text, images, audio, video, code or a combination of several formats.

The term “generative” distinguishes it from systems primarily designed to classify, detect or predict. An email filter can classify a message as spam. A generative model can draft a response to that message.

How a model learns

During training, a model analyses large amounts of information and adjusts its internal parameters to recognize relationships. It does not store a perfect library of ready-made answers. It learns regularities that allow it to construct a new output.

For a language model, generation involves estimating which fragment of text is most likely to continue the sequence. The process repeats until a complete response has been formed.

This is why an output can be coherent without necessarily being true. Linguistic coherence and factual accuracy are different things.

The role of the instruction

The instruction, commonly known as a prompt, provides context and guides the output. A vague request tends to produce a general response. An instruction that includes the objective, audience and constraints gives the model better signals.

Even so, writing a good prompt does not remove the need for review. The tool may misinterpret a condition, omit an important part or fill gaps with invented information.

What it can contribute to web development

In web development, AI can help explore code, explain an error, draft documentation or generate an initial proposal for tests. It can also help organize lengthy requirements and identify questions that still need answers.

Its greatest value appears when it speeds up exploration without hiding the verification process. If it suggests a solution, we still need to understand it, test it and assess whether it fits the project.

Copying code without reviewing it can introduce bugs, unnecessary dependencies or security problems. Using AI professionally means retaining technical responsibility.

Why hallucinations occur

A hallucination occurs when a model produces information that is incorrect, invented or out of context. It might create a reference that does not exist, attribute a quotation to the wrong person or claim that a function is available when it is not.

The problem is particularly subtle because the answer may sound convincing. Fluency is not proof of knowledge or certainty.

To reduce the risk, we can provide reliable context, ask the model to distinguish facts from assumptions and verify important information using original sources.

Privacy, bias and copyright

Before entering information into an AI tool, we should ask whether it contains personal data, client information, private code or confidential material.

Models can also reflect biases found in their training data. We therefore need to check whether a recommendation treats certain people unfairly or reproduces stereotypes.

Generating content does not remove questions about authorship and usage rights either. The terms of each tool and the publication context still matter.

Human oversight is still necessary

Oversight means more than correcting spelling mistakes. It means defining the objective, reviewing the reasoning, checking sources and taking responsibility for the result we ultimately use.

AI can make a proposal. The decision to accept, modify or reject it remains human.

Conclusion

Generative artificial intelligence can accelerate tasks, expand options and make complex knowledge easier to access. But it is not an automatic source of truth, nor does it replace professional experience.

Understanding how it works allows us to use it more effectively: with curiosity, but also with sound judgment. The important question is not only what AI can generate, but what we need to verify before using its output.
